The corporate website was long understood as a storefront.

That logic is weakening.

If the early stages of selection increasingly happen through AI agents, businesses begin to be compared not by impression, but by the structure of the facts available.

This shifts the focus. Not "how persuasive is the page", but "what in the business can not only be claimed, but verified".

It is here, it seems to me, that the new architectural boundary lies.

The website of the future is not a collection of pages, nor a separate API on the side. It is a verifiable representation of the business: a single source of truth from which both a person and an agent receive the same data.

In such a model, machine-readability is not in itself an advantage. If only price, lead times, and availability are structurally distinguishable, the business is more quickly pulled into product-level comparison.

The advantage emerges elsewhere: in verifiable, non-commoditizable attributes. Identity. Qualifications. History of completed work. Boundaries of responsibility. Signed assertions where there is risk and commitment.

From this follows a practical conclusion. It is not worth building a "website for people" and, separately, a "layer for agents". What is needed is one canonical model of the business and two projections of the same core.

At the same time, the human layer does not disappear. On the contrary. It remains at the points of irreversibility, responsibility, and confirmation.

In the article, I examine this logic as an engineering invariant, not as just another fashionable scenario.

If interfaces change, what in your business will survive that change: presentation or verifiability?
